title: HTTP Caching, Cookies & CORS
tagline: Cache-Control directives, ETags, cookie security flags (SameSite/HttpOnly/Secure), and CORS preflight — the HTTP features that control performance and security for every web request.

sections.content:
Every time a browser loads a page it makes a series of decisions that most developers never consciously think about: should this asset be fetched from the network or pulled from cache? Should this cookie travel with the request? Is this cross-origin API call even permitted? Three HTTP mechanisms answer these questions for every single request: **HTTP Caching**, **Cookies**, and **CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing).

**HTTP Caching** is the invisible performance layer of the web. A response stored in cache can be served in microseconds instead of the hundreds of milliseconds a real network round-trip takes. A well-cached web application loads its JavaScript bundle exactly once per deployment; a poorly-cached one fetches the same unchanging file on every page visit. The difference between a fast web app and a slow one is often mostly this.

**Cookies** solve a fundamental problem with HTTP: the protocol is stateless by design, meaning each request is independent and the server has no memory of previous requests. Cookies are the mechanism that adds state — they are small key-value stores the browser automatically attaches to matching requests. Without cookies there would be no 'stay logged in' checkbox, no shopping cart that persists across pages, no personalization of any kind. But cookies that are misconfigured are also one of the most common entry points for two of the web's most dangerous attack classes: XSS-based session theft and CSRF.

**CORS** exists because browsers implement the Same-Origin Policy, a fundamental security boundary that prevents a script on `attacker.com` from reading your emails at `gmail.com` via a fetch request. CORS is the system that allows servers to selectively punch a hole in this boundary — to say 'yes, `app.example.com` is allowed to read my responses'. It is often encountered as an annoying error message during development, but understanding why it exists makes the configuration obvious rather than cargo-culted.

This chapter goes deep on all three: the mechanics, the headers, the security reasoning behind each flag, the common mistakes, and the mental models that let you reason from first principles rather than trial-and-error.

sections.caption: The HTTP cache decision tree. Fresh cache means zero network round-trip. Stale cache triggers a conditional GET — a lightweight check that returns 304 (no body) when content is unchanged, saving bandwidth while guaranteeing freshness.

sections.title: A Library, a Library Card, and a Door Policy
sections.content:
**HTTP Caching** is like keeping a copy of a book at the front desk of a library:
- `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` is the librarian's note: 'This book is definitely current for the next hour — do not bother calling the publisher to verify.'
- `ETag` is the book's edition number stamped on the cover. When the hour expires, instead of ordering a whole new book, the librarian calls the publisher: 'I have edition #42 — has anything changed?' If not, the publisher says '304 — keep your copy.' Huge savings.
- `no-cache` means: 'Always call the publisher before lending this book, but you may keep the physical copy in case they confirm nothing changed.'
- `no-store` means: 'Do not keep any copy at all — shred it after the patron reads it. Fetch fresh every time.'
- `immutable` means: 'This book is a numbered collector's edition. The content will never change. You will never need to call the publisher again.'

**Cookies** are your library membership card — they identify you to the librarian on every visit without re-authentication. The card has security attributes:
- `HttpOnly` means the card lives in a sealed wallet only the building's readers can open. A thief who breaks into the reading room (XSS) cannot grab the card itself.
- `Secure` means the card is only accepted at branches with reinforced doors (HTTPS). A plaintext-HTTP branch won't transmit your card and expose it.
- `SameSite=Strict` means: 'Only show this card to this specific library chain. If someone from another town asks me to visit this library on their behalf (CSRF), I leave the card at home.'

**CORS** is the door policy. The building (browser) has a rule: people from Outside Town (cross-origin scripts) cannot read the library's private collection. But the library director (your server) can issue a special permit (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`) that explicitly grants Outside Town visitors access to specific shelves. The permit is checked at the door — the building enforces it, not the books themselves.

sections.title: HTTP Caching: The Cache-Control Header in Depth
sections.content:
The `Cache-Control` response header is the primary tool for controlling caching behaviour. It can carry multiple comma-separated directives that instruct both the browser cache and any intermediate caches (CDN, reverse proxy) on how to store and revalidate responses.

**Freshness directives**:
- `max-age=N` — the response is fresh for N seconds from the time it was created. During this window, the browser serves the cached copy without any network contact.
- `s-maxage=N` — like `max-age` but applies only to shared caches (CDNs, proxies). Lets you cache a resource in the CDN for 24 hours while giving browsers a shorter TTL.
- `stale-while-revalidate=N` — an advanced directive: serve the stale cached response immediately while simultaneously fetching a fresh one in the background. Users see the fast stale response; the next request will see the fresh one. Great for non-critical data like analytics dashboards.
- `stale-if-error=N` — if revalidation fails (server error, network down), serve the stale response for up to N additional seconds. Improves resilience.

**Storage directives**:
- `no-store` — the response must never be stored in any cache. Each request fetches from the origin. Use for sensitive responses: banking transactions, health records.
- `no-cache` — a notoriously confusing name. It does NOT mean 'do not cache'. It means 'you may store a copy, but you must revalidate with the server before serving it'. The server's `304 Not Modified` response then authorises serving the stored copy. Use for HTML entry points.
- `private` — only the end-user's browser may cache this. CDNs and shared proxies must not store it. Use for personalised or user-specific responses.
- `public` — any cache (including shared CDNs) may store this response, even if it came with an `Authorization` header.

**Validation directives**:
- `must-revalidate` — once the response is stale, caches must not serve it (not even under error conditions) until they revalidate with the origin.
- `immutable` — the content at this URL will never change. Browsers will not even send conditional revalidation requests during the `max-age` window. Use exclusively with content-hashed URLs like `app.a1b2c3.js`.

sections.title: ETags and Conditional Requests: Revalidation Without Full Download
sections.content:
When a cached response becomes stale, the browser does not blindly download the resource again. If the server sent an `ETag` or `Last-Modified` header with the original response, the browser can make a **conditional request** — essentially asking 'has anything changed since I last fetched this?'

**ETag** (Entity Tag) is an arbitrary string (often a hash of the content, or a version number) that uniquely identifies the current version of a resource. The server includes it in the response:

`ETag: "d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e"`

When the cached response becomes stale, the browser sends:

`If-None-Match: "d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e"`

If the resource hasn't changed, the server responds with `304 Not Modified` — no body, just headers. The browser reuses the cached body and resets the freshness timer. If the resource has changed, the server sends `200 OK` with the full new content and a new ETag.

**Last-Modified / If-Modified-Since** works the same way but uses a timestamp instead of a hash. Less precise (files can be modified and re-saved with the same content, bumping the timestamp unnecessarily) but widely supported and computationally cheaper for the server.

**Strong vs. Weak ETags**: A strong ETag (`"abc"`) means byte-for-byte identical content. A weak ETag (`W/"abc"`) means semantically equivalent (perhaps whitespace changed). Weak ETags cannot be used for range requests.

The practical implication: `no-cache` with ETags gives you the best of both worlds — you always check in with the server, but if nothing changed you pay only the RTT cost of the check, not the bandwidth cost of re-downloading the response body. For a 500 KB JavaScript bundle, that is the difference between ~2ms and ~400ms on a slow connection.

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant S as Server
    B->>S: GET /app.js (cold cache)
    S->>B: 200 OK, ETag: "v7", Cache-Control: no-cache
    Note over B: Stores response with ETag
    B->>S: GET /app.js (after cache expires)
    B->>S: If-None-Match: "v7"
    S->>B: 304 Not Modified (no body)
    Note over B: Reuses cached body, saves bandwidth

    S->>B: 200 OK, ETag: "v8", new content
sections.caption: ETag revalidation flow. The 304 path saves the full response body download — only headers travel over the network. On a large bundle, this is the difference between milliseconds and seconds.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The Fetch API's `cache` option mirrors `Cache-Control` semantics on the request side. `no-store` is the nuclear option — it bypasses cache in both directions. `no-cache` forces a conditional revalidation check but reuses the body if the server returns 304. On the server side, the cache strategy should be determined by the resource type — hashed assets benefit enormously from `immutable` while HTML entry points must always revalidate.

sections.title: Cookies: How They Work and Why Security Flags Exist
sections.content:
A cookie is a name-value pair that the server sends to the browser via the `Set-Cookie` response header. The browser stores it and automatically includes it in subsequent requests to matching URLs via the `Cookie` request header. This gives HTTP — which is inherently stateless — its memory.

**Setting a cookie from the server**:
`Set-Cookie: session_id=abc123; Max-Age=86400; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict`

Each attribute after the semicolons is a flag controlling the cookie's lifetime, scope, and security behaviour.

**Lifetime and scope**:
- `Max-Age=N` — cookie expires N seconds from now. Preferred over `Expires` (which uses an absolute date and suffers from clock skew).
- `Expires=date` — older form. Both set a persistent cookie; omitting both creates a session cookie that expires when the browser closes.
- `Domain=.example.com` — the cookie is sent to `example.com` and all its subdomains (`api.example.com`, `app.example.com`). Without this attribute, the cookie is sent only to the exact domain that set it.
- `Path=/admin` — the cookie is only sent for URLs under `/admin`. Useful for separating admin sessions from public sessions on the same domain.

**Security flags — the critical three**:
`HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite` form the security trinity for session cookies. Each protects against a specific attack vector.

**`HttpOnly`** prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie. `document.cookie` will not show `HttpOnly` cookies; `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` cannot read them either. They are transmitted by the browser automatically but are invisible to scripts. This single flag defeats the most common XSS attack pattern: injecting a `<script>` that reads `document.cookie` and exfiltrates the session token to an attacker-controlled server. Without `HttpOnly`, XSS = instant session hijacking.

**`Secure`** restricts cookie transmission to HTTPS connections only. On a plain HTTP connection (even `localhost` in production environments) the browser will not include a `Secure` cookie in requests. This prevents man-in-the-middle attacks on networks where traffic is not encrypted — coffee shop Wi-Fi, corporate proxies, DNS-based downgrade attacks.

**`SameSite`** controls whether the cookie is sent on cross-site requests, which is the core mechanism preventing CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery). CSRF is when an attacker on `evil.com` causes the victim's browser to make a state-changing request to `bank.com` (e.g., transfer money). Because the browser automatically includes cookies, the request arrives at the bank server looking fully authenticated.

- `SameSite=Strict` — the cookie is never sent on any cross-site request. Not even when the user clicks a link from another site to your site. Strongest protection, but can create friction (user clicks a link to your app from an email, and the initial load is treated as unauthenticated).
- `SameSite=Lax` — the browser default since ~2020. Sends the cookie on top-level navigation GET requests (clicking a link) but not on cross-site sub-resource requests (images, AJAX, iframes). Blocks most CSRF attacks while preserving the 'user clicks a link and arrives logged-in' experience.
- `SameSite=None; Secure` — explicitly allows cross-site sending. Required for embedded iframes, third-party widgets, and federated authentication flows where your cookie must be sent from inside a third-party context. The `Secure` flag is mandatory with `None`.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NoCookie: First request
    NoCookie --> CookieSet: Server sends Set-Cookie
    CookieSet --> SentWithRequest: Browser includes Cookie header
    SentWithRequest --> SentWithRequest: On each matching request
    SentWithRequest --> Expired: Max-Age elapsed

sections.caption: Cookie lifecycle: set by server, stored by browser, automatically sent on matching requests, deleted when expired or explicitly cleared. HttpOnly cookies are invisible in this cycle to JavaScript — only the browser's network layer touches them.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The most important line here is the comment about `HttpOnly`: it cannot be set from JavaScript because the entire point of the flag is to prevent JavaScript access. Server-side frameworks (Express, NestJS, Django, Rails) set it via the `Set-Cookie` response header. Session tokens should never go through `document.cookie` at all — they should live entirely in `HttpOnly` cookies, invisible to every script on the page.

sections.title: CORS: The Same-Origin Policy and Why It Exists
sections.content:
To understand CORS you first need to understand what it is responding to: the **Same-Origin Policy (SOP)**.

An **origin** is the combination of protocol, hostname, and port. `https://app.example.com:443` is a different origin from `https://api.example.com:443` (different subdomain), from `http://app.example.com:80` (different protocol and port), and from `https://app.example.com:8080` (different port).

The Same-Origin Policy prevents a script loaded from origin A from reading the response body of a request made to origin B. This is a browser-enforced security boundary. Without it, the following attack would work trivially: you visit `malicious.com`, which runs a script that fetches `https://yourbank.com/api/account-balance`. Because your browser has your bank session cookies, the request is authenticated. Without SOP, the script on `malicious.com` would be able to read the response — your account balance, then your transaction history, then trigger a transfer.

Note carefully: SOP prevents **reading** cross-origin responses. It does not prevent browsers from **making** cross-origin requests. The request goes out; only the response is blocked from the initiating script. This nuance matters for CSRF (where the attack goal is to cause an action, not read data) and for understanding what preflight actually guards against.

**CORS is the opt-in mechanism** for servers to selectively relax the Same-Origin Policy for specific trusted origins. The server asserts: 'Even though your SOP would normally block this, I authorise `https://app.example.com` to read my responses.'

Critically: CORS enforcement lives in the browser, not the server. The server still processes and responds to the request. The browser is what decides whether to let the calling JavaScript read the response. This means CORS is entirely bypassed by `curl`, Postman, server-to-server requests, or any non-browser HTTP client — those tools do not implement the Same-Origin Policy.

sections.title: CORS: Simple Requests vs. Preflight Requests
sections.content:
Browsers categorise cross-origin requests into two types with different CORS handling.

**Simple requests** skip the preflight and go directly to the server. To qualify as simple, a request must:
1. Use only `GET`, `POST`, or `HEAD`.
2. Only include headers in the 'CORS-safelisted' set: `Accept`, `Accept-Language`, `Content-Language`, `Content-Type` (but only with values `text/plain`, `multipart/form-data`, or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`).
3. Not use `ReadableStream` in the body.

For a simple request, the browser sends the request and checks the response for the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header. If it matches the requesting origin (or is `*`), the JavaScript receives the response. If it does not match, the browser blocks the response — a CORS error in the console.

**Non-simple (preflighted) requests** require the browser to first send an `OPTIONS` request — the **preflight** — to ask the server whether the actual request is permitted. Any of the following triggers a preflight:
- Methods other than GET/POST/HEAD: PUT, DELETE, PATCH
- Custom request headers: `Authorization`, `Content-Type: application/json`, any `X-Custom-*` header
- Using `ReadableStream`

The preflight `OPTIONS` request includes:
- `Origin: https://app.example.com`
- `Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT`
- `Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type`

The server must respond to this `OPTIONS` request with the appropriate `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers. If the preflight fails (wrong or missing headers), the browser never sends the actual request. If it succeeds, the actual request proceeds.

**`Access-Control-Max-Age`** is a performance optimisation: it tells the browser to cache the preflight result for N seconds. Without it, every non-simple cross-origin request requires an extra round-trip. With `max-age=86400` (24 hours), the browser sends the OPTIONS check at most once per day for that endpoint.

sequenceDiagram

    B->>S: OPTIONS /api/profile

sections.title: CORS Headers Reference and Credentials
sections.content:
**Server response headers for CORS**:
- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com` — the specific origin allowed to read responses. Use `*` for fully public APIs with no credentials. Only one origin can appear here (not a comma-separated list), so servers must dynamically reflect the requesting origin from a whitelist if multiple origins are allowed.
- `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH` — allowed HTTP methods.
- `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization, X-Request-ID` — headers the browser is permitted to send in the actual request.
- `Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Total-Count, X-Request-ID` — response headers that JavaScript is allowed to read. By default, only a small set of 'CORS-safelisted' response headers are readable by JS code; everything else is hidden even if the request succeeds.
- `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` — required if the request includes credentials (cookies, HTTP authentication). Without this, the browser strips cookies from the request.
- `Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400` — seconds to cache the preflight result.

**The credentials constraint** is one of the most misunderstood CORS rules: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` cannot be used together. Browsers will reject this combination with an error. The reason is security: a wildcard plus credentials would mean any website on the internet could make authenticated cross-origin requests using the victim's cookies. The server must echo back the specific requesting origin (e.g., `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com`) when credentials are involved.

**On the client side**, credentials are opt-in:
- `fetch(url, { credentials: 'omit' })` — never send cookies or auth headers (default for cross-origin requests)
- `fetch(url, { credentials: 'same-origin' })` — send cookies only for same-origin requests (default for same-origin)
- `fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' })` — always send cookies, even cross-origin (requires server cooperation)

sections.caption: The credentials + CORS constraint. Both conditions must hold: Allow-Credentials must be true AND Allow-Origin must be a specific origin (not *). The wildcard is intentionally incompatible with credentials to prevent any-site authenticated requests.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `Vary: Origin` header is easy to forget but critical for correctness when serving multiple origins: it tells CDNs to cache separate copies of the response for each Origin value. Without it, a CDN might cache a response with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com` and serve it to requests from `https://admin.example.com`, causing a CORS failure. The origin whitelist approach (checking against a Set of allowed origins and echoing back the matched one) is the standard pattern for multi-origin APIs with credentials.

sections.title: Edge Cases and Common Misconceptions
sections.content:
**'CORS is a server-side problem'** — Not quite. CORS enforcement is entirely browser-side. Server-to-server requests (microservices calling each other, `curl`, Postman) are completely unaffected by CORS headers. The server sends its response regardless; only the browser decides whether to give that response to the requesting JavaScript. This means a CORS error in the browser does not indicate the request failed — it indicates the browser blocked JavaScript from reading the response.

**'`no-cache` means do not cache'** — It does not. `no-cache` means 'store but always revalidate'. `no-store` means 'do not cache at all'. These are regularly confused even by experienced developers.

**'ETags are always content hashes'** — Not required by the spec. An ETag is any opaque string chosen by the server. It could be a database row version number, a timestamp, a hash, or a sequential counter. The spec only requires that different content has different ETags and identical content has the same ETag.

**'`SameSite=Strict` is always best'** — It provides the strongest CSRF protection but breaks important UX flows. If a user clicks an email link to `app.example.com`, the initial navigation is a cross-site request, and a `Strict` session cookie will not be sent. The user arrives at the page as if logged out, then gets redirected to login. For most applications, `SameSite=Lax` is the right balance.

**'CORS allows the browser to block requests'** — Browsers actually send the request in most cases (the exception is preflight-blocked scenarios). CORS controls whether JavaScript can read the response. This is why CSRF is a separate concern from CORS: a CSRF attack does not need to read the response — it just needs the side effect (state change) of the request to happen. `SameSite` cookies, not CORS, are the defense against CSRF.

**'Third-party cookie deprecation affects `SameSite=None`'** — Chrome and other browsers are phasing out third-party cookies (those sent in third-party contexts). Even `SameSite=None; Secure` cookies are being blocked in many contexts by browser tracking protections. Authentication flows that rely on cross-site cookies are increasingly moving to browser-native federated authentication APIs (FedCM, Storage Access API).

**Cache invalidation with CDNs** — `Cache-Control: max-age` directives cannot be revoked once a response is cached at a CDN edge node. If you cache a sensitive response with a long TTL and later discover it contains a bug, your only options are: (1) wait for the TTL to expire, (2) use CDN-specific purge APIs, or (3) use URL versioning so the cached URL is simply no longer requested. This is why long TTLs should only be used with content-hashed URLs.

**`Vary` header and CDN caching interactions**: When your server responds with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` dynamically (echoing the requesting origin), you must also include `Vary: Origin` in the response. Without it, a CDN will cache the first response (say, with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com`) and serve that same cached response — with the wrong Allow-Origin — to all subsequent requests regardless of their `Origin` header. `Vary: Origin` instructs the CDN to maintain separate cache entries for each distinct Origin value. Similarly, if your response varies by `Accept-Encoding`, include `Vary: Accept-Encoding`. The `Vary` header is the mechanism for making a single URL serve different responses to different clients correctly.

**Interview and production traps to know cold**:
- **Cookie security checklist for session tokens**: `HttpOnly` (no JS access), `Secure` (HTTPS only), `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` (CSRF protection). All three, every time. A session cookie missing any of these is a security vulnerability, not a style issue.
- **`no-cache` vs `no-store`**: `no-cache` = 'store but always check in'. `no-store` = 'never store'. The wrong one on a sensitive endpoint can expose user data; the wrong one on a static asset kills your cache hit rate.
- **CORS does not protect APIs from server-to-server requests** — it only governs browser-based cross-origin reads. Rate limiting, authentication, and authorization are what protect APIs from abuse.
- **`credentials: 'include'` + `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` = browser error** — you must echo the specific origin when credentials are involved.
- **Content-hashed assets + `immutable`** — the single highest-leverage caching win available to any web app. If your build tool produces content-hashed filenames, apply `max-age=31536000, immutable` and the browser will never download that asset again until it changes.
- **Preflight caching with `Access-Control-Max-Age`** — each OPTIONS round-trip adds one full network RTT (50-300ms depending on server distance). Cache preflights aggressively (86400 seconds = 24 hours) for high-traffic APIs.

items: **`Cache-Control: max-age=N`** tells browsers and CDNs how long a response is fresh with no network contact. Pair it with **`immutable`** for content-hashed assets (JS/CSS/fonts) to eliminate all revalidation overhead. Use **`no-cache`** for HTML entry points so new deployments are always picked up.

**ETags and `304 Not Modified`** enable efficient revalidation: the browser sends `If-None-Match` with the stored ETag; if unchanged, the server responds with 304 and no body, saving bandwidth while guaranteeing freshness. This is the correct pattern for `no-cache` resources.

**Cookie security requires three flags**: `HttpOnly` (JavaScript cannot read it — defeats XSS session theft), `Secure` (HTTPS only — prevents network interception), and `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` (prevents CSRF — controls whether the cookie travels on cross-site requests). All three are required for session cookies.

**The Same-Origin Policy** (protocol + domain + port must match) prevents cross-origin JavaScript from reading responses. **CORS** is the server-controlled opt-in that selectively relaxes this boundary via `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and related headers — enforced by browsers, invisible to `curl` or server-to-server requests.

**CORS preflight** (`OPTIONS` request) is sent automatically before non-simple cross-origin requests (PUT/DELETE/PATCH, custom headers like `Authorization`). Cache preflights with `Access-Control-Max-Age` to avoid a costly extra round-trip on every API call.

**Credentialed CORS** (`credentials: 'include'`) requires both `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` AND a specific (non-wildcard) `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on the server. Wildcards and credentials are mutually exclusive by browser security design.

**`Vary: Origin`** is mandatory when echoing the requesting origin dynamically in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` — it prevents CDNs from serving one origin's CORS headers to a different origin, which would cause silent CORS failures for cached responses.

quiz.question: What does `Cache-Control: no-cache` actually mean?
options: Never cache this response under any circumstances
Store the response but always revalidate with the server before using it
Cache for 0 seconds (expire immediately on storage)
Only allow browser caching, not CDN caching
quiz.explanation: no-cache is one of the most confusingly named directives in HTTP. It does NOT mean 'do not cache'. It means 'you may store a copy, but you must send a conditional request (If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since) to the server before serving it'. If the server returns 304, the stored body is used. no-store is the directive that actually prevents any caching.

quiz.question: Which combination of Cache-Control directives is correct for a content-hashed JavaScript bundle like `app.a1b2c3d4.js`?
options: no-cache
no-store
max-age=3600
max-age=31536000, immutable
quiz.explanation: Content-hashed assets change their filename when content changes — the URL is the cache-busting mechanism. Since the URL will never serve different content, it is safe to cache indefinitely (max-age=31536000 = 1 year). The immutable directive tells browsers to skip even conditional revalidation requests during the max-age window, eliminating all unnecessary network contact for these assets.

quiz.question: What does the `HttpOnly` cookie attribute protect against?
options: Cookies being sent over unencrypted HTTP connections
JavaScript reading the cookie, which prevents XSS-based session token theft
Cross-site request forgery attacks
Cookies being stored on shared/public devices
quiz.explanation: HttpOnly makes the cookie invisible to JavaScript — document.cookie does not show it, fetch cannot read it, no script can access it. This directly defeats the most common XSS exploit: injecting a script that reads document.cookie and sends the session token to an attacker's server. The Secure flag (not HttpOnly) controls whether the cookie is sent over HTTPS only. SameSite (not HttpOnly) controls CSRF.

quiz.question: When does a browser send a CORS preflight (OPTIONS) request?
options: On every cross-origin request, without exception
Only when the server explicitly requests a preflight via a response header
For cross-origin requests that use non-simple methods (PUT/DELETE/PATCH) or non-safelisted headers (like Authorization)
Only for cross-origin POST requests with a JSON body
quiz.explanation: Simple requests (GET/POST/HEAD with only safelisted headers and safe Content-Type values) skip the preflight. Non-simple requests — PUT, DELETE, PATCH, or any request with custom headers like Authorization or Content-Type: application/json — trigger a preflight OPTIONS request first. The browser asks the server 'are you willing to accept this kind of request from this origin?' before sending the actual request.

quiz.question: What HTTP status code does a server return when a conditional GET (ETag revalidation) finds the resource has NOT changed?
options: 200 OK with an empty body
204 No Content
304 Not Modified
200 OK with the full resource body
quiz.explanation: 304 Not Modified tells the browser that the resource matches the version in its cache (the ETags matched). No body is sent in the response — the browser reuses the stored body. This is highly efficient: only a small HTTP response travels the network instead of the full resource, saving bandwidth while guaranteeing the cached content is still current.

quiz.question: Why can `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` NOT be combined with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`?
options: The wildcard character is not valid in CORS headers
Allowing credentials from any origin would let any website make authenticated cross-origin requests using the user's cookies — browsers block this by design
The wildcard only applies to GET and HEAD methods, not credentialed requests
Credentials require SameSite=None cookies, which conflict with the wildcard origin
quiz.explanation: A wildcard Allow-Origin combined with Allow-Credentials would mean any website on the internet could make cross-origin requests carrying the user's session cookies. This would fundamentally break the Same-Origin Policy's security guarantees. Browsers enforce that when credentials are involved, the server must reflect a specific, explicit origin — confirming it has made a deliberate choice to trust that particular origin with credentialed requests.

quiz.question: What does `SameSite=Lax` (the browser default since ~2020) allow?
options: Cookies sent on all cross-origin requests including AJAX and images
Cookies sent only on exact same-site requests (never cross-site)
Cookies sent on top-level cross-site navigations (GET links) but blocked on cross-site sub-resource requests
Cookies sent on any HTTPS request regardless of origin
quiz.explanation: SameSite=Lax sends the cookie when the user clicks a link that navigates the top-level page to your site (a cross-site GET navigation). It blocks the cookie on cross-site sub-resource requests like AJAX calls, images fetched by other sites, and iframe loads. This blocks most CSRF attacks while preserving the user experience of arriving at your site logged in after clicking a link in an email.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the `Access-Control-Max-Age` response header?
options: Sets how long the resource itself can be cached by the browser
Caches the preflight (OPTIONS) result so browsers skip the OPTIONS request for subsequent matching requests during that period
Sets the maximum TTL for session cookies issued in the same response
Controls how long a CORS permission is valid before the server must re-issue it
quiz.explanation: Access-Control-Max-Age tells the browser to cache the preflight response for N seconds. During this window, the browser skips the OPTIONS pre-check and sends the actual non-simple request directly. This is a significant performance optimization — each OPTIONS preflight is an extra full network round-trip (50-300ms). Setting Max-Age to 86400 means at most one OPTIONS per 24 hours per endpoint.

quiz.question: You set `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` dynamically by echoing the requesting origin from a whitelist. What other header must you include to prevent CDN caching issues?
options: Cache-Control: no-store
Vary: Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
X-Frame-Options: DENY
quiz.explanation: When the server dynamically reflects the requesting origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, responses to different origins are different. Without Vary: Origin, a CDN might cache the response for origin A and serve it (with A's Allow-Origin header) to requests from origin B, causing CORS failures for origin B. Vary: Origin tells CDNs to maintain separate cache entries for each distinct Origin value, ensuring each origin gets its own correctly-set CORS headers.

quiz.question: What is the Same-Origin Policy, and what does it actually restrict?
options: A server-side rule that blocks requests from different domains at the network level
A browser security rule that prevents JavaScript from reading responses from a different origin (protocol + domain + port), not from making requests
An HTTP specification requiring all API requests to originate from the same server
A CDN policy that only caches responses that originate from the registered domain
quiz.explanation: The Same-Origin Policy is a browser-enforced rule that prevents JavaScript on one origin from reading HTTP responses from a different origin (where origin = protocol + domain + port). Crucially, it restricts reading responses, not making requests — the browser still sends the request, only the script is denied access to the response body. This is why CSRF is a separate attack: CSRF exploits the fact that requests go through even without reading the response. CORS is the mechanism servers use to selectively allow specific cross-origins to read their responses.
